claim: Recent advances in mass spectrometry (MS) have enabled quantitative proteomics to become a powerful tool in the field of drug discovery, especially when applied toward proteome-wide target engagement studies.
source: Recent advances in mass spectrometry (MS) have enabled quantitative proteomics to become a powerful tool in the field of drug discovery, especially when applied toward proteome-wide target engagement studies.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Increasing concentrations of organic solvents stimulate unfolding and precipitation of the cellular proteome.
source: Similar to temperature gradients, increasing concentrations of organic solvents stimulate unfolding and precipitation of the cellular proteome.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Solvent-induced precipitation can be influenced by physical association with ligands and other molecules, making individual proteins more or less susceptible to solvent-induced denaturation.
source: This property can be influenced by physical association with ligands and other molecules, making individual proteins more or less susceptible to solvent-induced denaturation.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results showing compound-dependent shifts in melting curves (Figures 2-4) and builds on the principles from Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Solvent proteome profiling (SPP) is capable of establishing target engagement through analysis of SPP denaturation curves.
source: Using this approach, we developed solvent proteome profiling (SPP), which is capable of establishing target engagement through analysis of SPP denaturation curves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2 showing identification of known targets for SCIO-469, Alisertib, and MK2206.

claim: SPP readily identified the specific targets of compounds with known mechanisms of action.
source: We readily identified the specific targets of compounds with known mechanisms of action.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results in Figure 2 showing identification of MAPK14, MAPK12, AURKA, AKT1, and AKT2 as targets of their respective inhibitors.

claim: Solvent proteome integral solubility alteration (solvent-PISA) can serve as a reliable surrogate for SPP.
source: As a further efficiency boost, we applied the concept of area under the curve analysis to develop solvent proteome integral solubility alteration (solvent-PISA) and demonstrate that this approach can serve as a reliable surrogate for SPP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing that solvent-PISA identifies similar targets as SPP.

claim: Combining SPP with thermal proteome profiling can increase the absolute number of high-quality melting curves attainable by either approach individually.
source: We propose that by combining SPP with alternative methods, like thermal proteome profiling, it will be possible to increase the absolute number of high-quality melting curves that are attainable by either approach individually, thereby increasing the fraction of the proteome that can be screened for evidence of ligand binding.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 5 showing that combining SPP and TPP yields over 6400 high-quality curves compared to ~5000 for either method alone.

claim: The majority of the HCT116 proteome denatures between 0 and 25% AEA concentration.
source: While some proteins were insensitive to AEA treatment, the majority of the proteome appeared to denature well between the concentrations tested, reaching a bottom plateau around 25% AEA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the SDS-PAGE and BCA assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 8500 proteins were quantified in each replicate of the initial SPP experiment.
source: In total, we were able to quantify approximately 8500 proteins in each replicate, with greater than 7600 proteins being quantified in both 16plexes (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High-quality melting curves were fit to 6623 and 6879 proteins in replicates 1 and 2, respectively, using criteria of R² > 0.8 and plateau < 0.3.
source: Using these filters, we were able to fit high-quality melting curves to 6623 and 6879 proteins in each replicate, respectively, with a total of 5894 curves passing filters in both replicates (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The median CM in the initial SPP experiments was 10.2%, with an overall range of approximately 7–21% AEA.
source: The median CM in each experiment was 10.2%, with an overall range of approximately 7–21% AEA (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the CM distribution shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Individual CM values correlated well between replicates with a Pearson correlation of 0.9.
source: Individual CM values correlated well between replicates (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the correlation plot in Figure 1E showing Pearson correlation of 0.9.

claim: Approximately 78% of the detected cellular proteome can be assigned CM values using SPP.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that SIP can be employed to reliably and reproducibly assign CM values to a large fraction (~78%) of the cellular proteome that we were able to detect.
evidence: This is calculated from the data showing that ~6600-6900 proteins out of ~8500 quantified proteins received high-quality curves.

claim: SCIO-469 is an inhibitor of p38 MAP kinases.
source: To test this workflow, we selected SCIO-469, an inhibitor of p38 MAP kinases, for analysis by SPP (Dominguez et al., 2005; Hideshima et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dominguez et al., 2005 and Hideshima et al., 2004.

claim: MAPK14, MAPK13, and MAPK12 exhibited an evident shift in CM in response to SCIO-469 treatment.
source: Appropriately, all three of the p38 MAP kinases that we detected—MAPK14, MAPK13, and MAPK12—exhibited an evident shift in CM in response to SCIO-469 treatment (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the melting curves shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The compound-dependent stabilization of p38 by SCIO-469 was independently corroborated by western blot.
source: Additionally, the compound-dependent stabilization of p38 was independently corroborated by western blot, thereby validating the MS-based quantitation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Alisertib is a potent and specific inhibitor of AURKA, which it inhibits with at least two orders of magnitude greater potency than Aurora kinase B (AURKB).
source: Alisertib is a potent and specific inhibitor of AURKA, which it inhibits with at least two orders of magnitude greater potency than Aurora kinase B (AURKB) (Bavetsias and Linardopoulos, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bavetsias and Linardopoulos, 2015.

claim: Alisertib induces an evident shift in CM for AURKA, while AURKB did not experience such a shift.
source: Consistent with this disparity, Alisertib induces an evident shift in CM for AURKA, while AURKB did not experience such a shift in response to the compound (Figure 2C and E, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the melting curves shown in Figure 2C and western blot in Figure 2E.

claim: MK2206 is a pan-AKT inhibitor that causes a significant shift in both AKT1 and AKT2.
source: MK2206 is a pan-AKT inhibitor and, as such, causes a significant shift in both AKT1 and AKT2 (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirai et al., 2010 and the experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: High-quality solvent melting curves can be generated from just eight concentrations of AEA.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that high-quality solvent melting curves can be generated from just eight concentrations of AEA.
evidence: This is supported by the SPP data in Figure 2 showing that ~75% of quantified proteins received high-quality curves using 8 concentrations.

claim: Solvent-PISA requires just two TMTpro channels to compare a single compound to a vehicle-treated control, whereas the analogous SPP experiment would use the full 16 channels.
source: Importantly, comparing a single compound to a vehicle-treated control using solvent-PISA requires just two TMTpro channels (each channel represents thousands of melting curves from a single sample), whereas the analogous SPP experiment would use the full 16 channels.
evidence: This is based on the experimental design described in Figure 3A and the methods section.

claim: Solvent-PISA identified MAPK14 and MAPK12 as significant hits in response to SCIO-469 treatment.
source: In total, we quantified ~7200 proteins with two or more peptides and found that the known targets of SCIO-469, including MAPK14 and MAPK12, emerged as significant hits (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the volcano plot in Figure 3B.

claim: SCIO-469 can inhibit MAPK9/JNK2 as confirmed by in vitro kinase assay.
source: Therefore, we sought to confirm this result using an in vitro kinase assay and found that SCIO-469 could inhibit MAPK9/JNK2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the kinase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Greater than 97.5% of the solvent-PISA and thermal-PISA data had CVs under 15% across all groups.
source: In order to compare the two approaches (which used a varying number of replicates), we first calculated a %CV for each group and found that >97.5% of the data had CVs under 15% across all groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MAPK14, MAPK12, and MAPK9 had altered AUC values in both solvent-PISA and thermal-PISA assays in response to SCIO-469.
source: For example, MAPK14, MAPK12, and MAPK9 had altered AUC values in both assays in response to SCIO-469 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Following treatment with vorinostat, five proteins including two known targets HDAC1 and HDAC2 were among the largest fold changes in both solvent-PISA and thermal-PISA datasets.
source: Following treatment with vorinostat, five proteins, including two known targets HDAC1 and HDAC2, were among the largest fold changes in both datasets.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: MAPK8 and CDK19 are altered exclusively in solvent-PISA upon SCIO-469 treatment.
source: MAPK8 and CDK19, for example, are altered exclusively in solvent-PISA upon SCIO-469 treatment, while HDAC6 is altered exclusively in thermal-PISA following vorinostat treatment (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HDAC6 is altered exclusively in thermal-PISA following vorinostat treatment.
source: MAPK8 and CDK19, for example, are altered exclusively in solvent-PISA upon SCIO-469 treatment, while HDAC6 is altered exclusively in thermal-PISA following vorinostat treatment (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SPP and TPP appear to be complementary because one method could potentially identify a target that the other might miss.
source: Therefore, SPP and TPP appear to be complimentary not only because they can provide independent corroboration but because one method could potentially identify a target that the other might miss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some proteins are altered exclusively in one method but not the other, as shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: AURKA reached a maximum log2 fold change at the lowest dose of Alisertib assayed (5 μM) and held steady upon treatment with increasing doses.
source: AURKA reached a maximum log2 fold change at the lowest dose of Alisertib assayed and held steady upon treatment with increasing doses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment with increasing concentrations of MK2206 resulted in a dose-dependent increase in log2 fold change for AKT1 and AKT2.
source: Treatment with increasing concentrations of MK2206, on the other hand, resulted in a dose-dependent increase in log2 fold change for its targets—AKT1 and AKT2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The selection of AEA concentration range impacts the fold change values measured in solvent-PISA experiments, with higher and smaller windows generally resulting in larger fold changes.
source: Echoing what was seen previously for thermal-PISA, the selection of %AEA range had a profound impact on the ultimate log2 fold changes that were measured, with progressively later and smaller windows resulting in larger fold change values (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4D comparing different AEA windows.

claim: The calculated and measured log2 fold change values for different AEA windows were quite similar.
source: Having previously performed SPP on MK2206-treated lysates, we took the opportunity to calculate the expected log2 fold change for each %AEA window based on the SPP melting curves (Figure 2D) and found that the calculated (Figure 4D) and measured (Figure 4E) log2 fold change values were quite similar.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparing the data in Figure 4D and Figure 4E.

claim: CHEK1 only experienced a significant fold change in the smallest solvent-PISA window (14-19% AEA, window 4).
source: Indeed, CHEK1 does not appear to change substantially in any of the first three windows but exhibits an average log2 fold change of –0.7 upon utilization of window 4 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CHEK1 has a high CM and treatment with 25 µM MK2206 resulted in a slight but reproducible ΔCM.
source: Upon closer inspection of SPP data, it is clear that CHEK1 has a high CM and treatment with 25 µM MK2206 resulted in a slight but reproducible ΔCM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the melting curves shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Treatment with 125 µM MK2206 caused a significant decrease (log2 fold change of –0.52) in CHEK1 when utilizing the 9-19% AEA window.
source: Finally, we found that treatment with higher doses of MK2206 (125 µM) in an independent experiment caused a significant decrease (log2 fold change of –0.52) in CHEK1, even when utilizing the window of 9–19% AEA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: High-quality curves cannot be fit to as much as 30% of quantified proteins in TPP and SPP.
source: On the basis of previously published TPP data and the SPP data presented here, it appears that high-quality curves cannot be fit to as much as 30% of quantified proteins (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Jarzab et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, as well as citation to Jarzab et al., 2020.

claim: Approximately 8500 proteins were quantified in both SPP and TPP experiments performed on HCT116 lysates.
source: Each approach resulted in the quantification of ~8500 proteins.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text describing the combined SPP and TPP experiment.

claim: 25-30% of SPP and TPP datasets were lost due to poor curve quality, meaning only approximately 6500 proteins could be assigned a CM or TM.
source: However, 25–30% of each dataset were lost due to poor curve quality, meaning that only approximately 6500 proteins could be assigned a CM or TM (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: A total of 7667 proteins were quantified using both SPP and TPP.
source: A total of 7667 proteins were quantified using both SPP and TPP.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: High-quality curves could be fit to approximately 5000 proteins in both SPP and TPP approaches.
source: Using R2 > 0.8 and plateau < 0.3 as criteria, high-quality curves could be fit to approximately 5000 proteins in both approaches, while over 1000 proteins could not be assigned a good curve using either SPP or TPP (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Over 620 proteins produced high-quality curves in SPP but not TPP.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, there were over 620 proteins that produced high-quality curves in SPP but not TPP and over 850 proteins that produced high-quality curves in TPP but not SPP.
evidence: This is directly stated and can be inferred from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Over 850 proteins produced high-quality curves in TPP but not SPP.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, there were over 620 proteins that produced high-quality curves in SPP but not TPP and over 850 proteins that produced high-quality curves in TPP but not SPP.
evidence: This is directly stated and can be inferred from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: By combining both SPP and TPP, high-quality curves could be fit to a total of over 6400 proteins, which is more than either approach independently.
source: Therefore, by combining both SPP and TPP, we were able to fit high-quality curves to a total of over 6400 proteins, which is more than either approach, independently (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SPP and solvent-PISA represent a significant advancement compared to the previous iteration of solvent-induced precipitation (SIP).
source: Using the principles of SIP as a foundation (Zhang et al., 2020), we have developed proteome-wide solvent shift assays in the form of SPP and solvent-PISA, which represent a significant advancement compared to the previous iteration.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript showing proteome-wide analysis capabilities not present in the original SIP method.

claim: Methods to fit protein abundance data with sigmoidal melting curves facilitate the assignment of CM values to a significant fraction of the cellular proteome.
source: Furthermore, we present methods to fit protein abundance data with sigmoidal melting curves, which facilitates the assignment of CM values to a significant fraction of the cellular proteome (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data in Figure 1 showing CM assignments for ~6600-6900 proteins.

claim: SPP can encounter challenges in fitting and analyzing melting curves, similar to TPP.
source: Upon analysis of SPP data, we found that it was possible to assign high-quality melting curves and CM values to a similar but nonredundant proportion of the total proteome compared to TPP. Furthermore, like TPP, SPP can encounter challenges in fitting and analyzing melting curves.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that MAPK14 and AURKA shifted CM to the point where they failed curve quality filters, as described in the Discussion.

claim: Solvent-PISA can overcome poor curve quality to some extent, as both MAPK14 and AURKA were recovered as statistically significant hits.
source: In terms of solvent-PISA, we were again able to cover a similar fraction of the proteome and demonstrate that, in comparison to thermal-PISA, it is generally possible to identify a similar set of targets in response to compound treatment. Solvent-PISA can also overcome poor curve quality to some extent as both MAPK14 and AURKA were recovered as statistically significant hits in solvent-PISA (Figure 3B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SPP and solvent-PISA are not amenable to cell-based approaches like CETSA because the plasma membrane will likely impede the ability of AEA to access the cellular proteome of living cells.
source: This is because, unlike heat, the plasma membrane will likely impede the ability of AEA to access with the cellular proteome of living cells, thereby preventing solvent-induced protein precipitation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the chemical properties of AEA and the barrier function of the plasma membrane.

claim: Utilizing additional means of proteome denaturation like salt, acid, additional solvents, and chemical denaturants could allow access to a greater number of high-quality curves.
source: Utilizing additional means of proteome denaturation like salt, acid, additional solvents, chemical denaturants, and others could allow access to a greater number of high-quality curves (Meng et al., 2018; Savitski et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Altering proteome extraction conditions could increase proteomic coverage in SPP and TPP experiments.
source: Additionally, altering proteome extraction conditions could also increase the proteomic coverage. In this report, we generated all native cell lysates using 0.5% NP-40. However, these assays are amenable to a myriad of extraction strategies (Reinhard et al., 2015; Savitski et al., 2014; Sridharan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to relevant literature showing different extraction strategies.

claim: Maximizing the fraction of the proteome that can be captured with high-quality curves will benefit PISA-type approaches.
source: While AUC approaches (PISA) do not explicitly rely on building curves to determine engagement, these curves are still important, and while it remains formally possible that PISA could overcome poor curve quality, more high-quality curves will still ultimately prove beneficial. Therefore, maximizing the fraction of the proteome that can be captured with high-quality curves will also benefit PISA-type approaches.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between curve quality and PISA performance.

claim: SPP could serve as a suitable alternative for anyone that is unable to perform TPP.
source: While we ultimately consider SPP and TPP to be complimentary approaches, we propose that SPP could serve as a suitable alternative for anyone that is unable to perform TPP.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the demonstrated capabilities of SPP shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: HCT116 cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1× penicillin-streptomycin.
source: HCT116 cells (purchased from ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1× penicillin-streptomycin.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used.

claim: HCT116 cells were confirmed to be mycoplasma negative.
source: HCT116 cells were confirmed to be mycoplasma negative.
evidence: This is a direct statement of quality control performed on the cell line.

claim: HCT116 proteomes were extracted from frozen cell pellets with lysis buffer containing 1× TBS, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.5% NP-40, and 1× protease inhibitor.
source: HCT116 proteomes were extracted from frozen cell pellets with lysis buffer (1× TBS, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.5% NP-40, 1× protease inhibitor [Pierce Protease Inhibitor Mini Tablets]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used.

claim: In SPP experiments, samples were incubated with compound or vehicle for 15 min at room temperature before AEA treatment.
source: Compound (solubilized in DMSO) or DMSO was added to the desired concentration, and the samples were allowed to incubate at RT for 15 min.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental protocol.

claim: AEA-treated samples were incubated at 37°C with vigorous shaking for 20 min in SPP experiments.
source: Upon addition of AEA, samples were incubated at 37°C with vigorous shaking for 20 min.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental protocol.

claim: In TPP experiments, samples were heated across a temperature gradient from 38 to 61°C for 3 min.
source: Each sample was divided into eight aliquots and heated across a temperature gradient from 38 to 61°C for 3 min in an Eppendorf Mastercycler Pro S.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental protocol.

claim: The TPP R package (3.17.6) was adapted to enable the analysis of SPP data.
source: The TPP R package (3.17.6) (Franken et al., 2015) was adapted to enable the analysis of SPP data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the computational methods used, supported by citation to Franken et al., 2015.

claim: Proteins for generating normalization curves in SPP met specific criteria including that the 5th point was between 0.4 and 0.6 for 8-point curves.
source: Proteins for generating normalization curves met the following criteria: (i) the 5th (8-point curves) or 10th (16-point curves) point was between 0.4 and 0.6; (ii) the 7th (8-point curves) or 15th (16-point curves) point was between 0 and 0.3; and (iii) the last point was between 0 and 0.2.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis criteria.

claim: High-quality curves were designated as those with R² > 0.8, plateau < 0.3, valid slopes, and valid melting/denaturation points.
source: Following the criteria used in the published TPP protocol (Franken et al., 2015), we designated curves with R2 > 0.8, plateau < 0.3, valid slopes, and valid melting/denaturation points as high-quality curves.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the quality criteria used, supported by citation to Franken et al., 2015.

claim: Significant hits in SPP were designated as proteins fulfilling all four quality requirements with adjusted p-values<0.001 and peptides > 1 in both replicates.
source: Significant hits are designated as proteins fulfilling all four requirements (fulfills_all_4_requirements="Yes", see Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1–3, Figure 5—source data 1 for details), with adjusted p-values<0.001 and peptides > 1 in both replicates.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical criteria used for identifying significant hits.

claim: Significant changes in solvent-PISA were determined using a permutation-based FDR with settings of FDR = 0.05, S0 = 0.1, and number of randomizations = 250.
source: Significant changes were determined using a permutation-based FDR with the following settings: FDR – 0.05, S0 – 0.1, and number of randomizations – 250.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical methods used.

claim: The median CM in SPP experiments using 8 concentrations was approximately 12%, in contrast to ~10% observed with 16 concentrations.
source: Using these eight-point melting curves, we next assigned a CM to each protein in the control and treated groups and found a median CM of approximately 12% across all four groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–H). This is in contrast to the median CM of ~10%, which was observed in Figure 1.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: The disparity in median CM between experiments stems from day-to-day variation in the preparation of AEA stock solutions.
source: We believe that this disparity stems from day-to-day variation in the preparation of AEA stock solutions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in median CM values.

claim: Replicate SPP data produced using identical AEA stocks generate CM values that are highly reproducible.
source: Nonetheless, while there appears to be some amount of deviation between experiments, replicate data, produced using the identical AEA stocks, generate CM values that are highly reproducible (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I and J).
evidence: This is directly supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I and J.

claim: Proteins with reduced quality curves in SPP are enriched for Gene Ontology terms including plasma membrane, extracellular region, and lysosome.
source: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of proteins to which sigmoidal curves could not be fit well in replicate 1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B displaying GO enrichment results.
